title: Minecraft Voxel Sandbox
text:
BENCHMARK EXECUTION CONTRACT

Run identity / isolation
- Model: `ox-alpha`.
- All project files must live under `C:\Users\Epic\Documents\ChatGPT\Ox model test`.
- Required folder: `<Project Name> [model:ox-alpha] [<harness-key>] [run:<NN>]`.
- Use a short lowercase harness key. Start at `run:01`; if that project/model/harness already exists, atomically claim the next available two-digit run number.
- Never overwrite, reuse, rename over, or modify another run's folder. Keep project dependencies/artifacts inside this run folder where practical.

Browser-only + parallel testing
- Finished project must run in a standard modern browser. Local dev servers are fine; Electron/Tauri/native runtimes are not substitutes.
- Assume many runs test simultaneously. Use a unique free localhost port, isolated browser profile/context, and run-scoped temp/cache/download/trace/screenshot artifacts.
- Never hijack, navigate, close, or kill unrelated browser tabs/processes/servers, and never kill something merely to free a port.
- Track/clean up only resources created by this run. Prefer headless testing unless visible interaction is genuinely required.

- Keep critical runtime assets/dependencies local or bundled when practical so the finished project does not unnecessarily depend on fragile third-party CDNs/APIs just to boot.
- Handle browser user-gesture restrictions correctly for features such as audio, fullscreen, pointer lock, clipboard, autoplay, or similar browser-gated capabilities; provide a clear user action instead of silently failing.
- If the project has non-obvious controls or shortcuts, expose them clearly in the experience through a controls/help overlay, onboarding hint, pause/menu screen, or similarly discoverable UI.

Execution efficiency
- Prefer the shortest direct implementation path that satisfies the task; investigate only enough to unblock building.
- Batch related checks when practical. Use bounded retries and switch strategy when an approach repeatedly fails.
- Preserve working progress. Finish the core vertical slice before extras.
- Avoid scope creep, prolonged architecture archaeology, over-debugging non-blockers, and stalling on optional services/assets; use sensible local/generated/mock fallbacks when useful.
- Verify real functionality, but do not run huge regression/stress/profiling suites unless a discovered issue warrants them.

Quality + performance
- Build a polished, coherent finished experience, not a checklist demo.
- Prioritize usability, visual quality, interaction feel, responsive feedback, consistent styling, and sensible design decisions.
- Avoid unfinished/debug/placeholder-looking final states when better treatment materially improves the result.
- Implement important behavior for real rather than faking it for screenshots. Keep code organized without overengineering.
- Keep runtime smooth/resource-conscious: avoid unbounded objects/effects/listeners/workers/requests, unnecessary per-frame work, runaway CPU/GPU/memory use, oversized assets, and performance that degrades over time.
- Reuse/pool/batch/cull/pause/clean up work when useful. Optimize the actual experience, not synthetic numbers, and do not sacrifice meaningful quality just to chase metrics.

Optional capabilities
- You may use any additional input modalities, inspection capabilities, or environment-provided tools when genuinely useful. Their use is optional; do not create extra work simply because they exist.

OPTIONAL CAPABILITY — ISOLATED E2E TESTING (contested-machine browser protocol)
If this run does any browser automation / E2E testing / screenshots and
{{E2E_ISOLATION_SKILL_PATH}} is not UNAVAILABLE, read and follow that SKILL.md
before your first browser/playwright step. Core rules it enforces: prefer
deterministic non-browser tests; ONE tab maximum (a second client is a raw
in-page WebSocket or node script, never a second tab); stamp every tab
(window.__TID) and re-assert stamp+URL before EVERY browser tool call;
abandon silently any tab showing someone else's page; keep trigger→assert
steps atomic under UI fade/expiry windows; clean up only process PIDs you
recorded spawning — never name-filter sweeps. Skill artifacts stay inside
this run's project folder. If the path is UNAVAILABLE, proceed using the
isolation rules above.

IMAGE GENERATION — USE THIS SKILL, NOTHING ELSE
If image generation/editing would genuinely help, use only:
`C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs`
No API keys or browser automation for image generation.

Rules:
- Node 18+; always pass `-o`; parse stdout exactly.
- Do not wrap/parallelize the script or create sleep-loop retry logic; keep `--delay-ms >= 1500`.
- Plus capacity is limited (~50 images/3h), so wait instead of retry-spamming limits.
- On 401, tell the user to run `codex login`.
- Sizes: `1024x1024|1024x1536|1536x1024`; quality: `low|medium|high`.

Single:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" -o out.png "PROMPT"`
Successful stdout = exactly one line, the absolute PNG path.

Batch:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" --n 10 --quality low -o sheet.png "PROMPT"`
Outputs `sheet-1.png`...`sheet-10.png`; exit `0` all ok / `2` partial / `1` fail; logs on stderr.

Edit:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" --ref input.png -o out.png "INSTRUCTION"`

For >3 images/background work:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue add [-o x.png] "PROMPT"`
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue run --detach`
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue status --json`
Poll about every 20s until `pending==0 && running==0`.
Use `queue list --json` for `.path`/`.error`; retry failed items with `queue run --retry-failed`.

CONDITIONAL MULTIPLAYER BUILD CONTRACT v2
Applies only if multiplayer is included. Epic handles deployment; you build only.
- Produce ONE self-contained static build folder suitable for `OxAlpha/<Project>/<Harness>/`.
- Do NOT deploy, push, SSH, edit compose files, touch Traefik, or run anything on the server.
- Multiplayer build folder: `<Project>-<Harness>` (Hermes harness unless told otherwise).
- Entry: root `index.html`, or `public/index.html` with that structure intact.
- `arcade.json` beside entry:
  `{"title":"<Human Name>","description":"<one line>","multiplayer":{"endpoint":"/ws/<project-slug>"}}`
- Slug must be lowercase `[a-z0-9-]` and match the `server.mjs` route exactly.

Optional backend:
- If needed, add ONE `server.mjs` beside entry: ESM, Node builtins only, no npm packages, no `listen()`, no spawned server.
- Platform loads a default export with optional `maxSockets`, optional `tickMs`, and `create(ctx)` returning `open`, `message`, `close`, optional `tick`, optional `stop`.
- `ws` provides `{ id, send(obj|string), close(code), query(URLSearchParams), ip }`.
- State is memory-only; clients reconnect/rejoin after restart. Keep handlers deterministic/fast. If offline-only, omit `server.mjs`.

Client netcode:
- Same-origin/subpath-safe only:
  `const url=(location.protocol==="https:"?"wss://":"ws://")+location.host+"/ws/<project-slug>";`
- Never hardcode domains/ports/`ws://localhost` or root-absolute asset/worker/importScripts paths.
- Auto-reconnect with backoff and graceful disconnected UI.
- Netcode belongs in normal source dirs.
- Game must still boot pure-static if backend is down, and from `file://` or a dumb static server.

Multiplayer handoff: state Project, Harness, entry path, endpoint, and message protocol/event payloads.

FINAL VERIFICATION / HANDOFF
- Launch the real project in a browser and exercise the core experience enough to catch obvious blockers.
- Screenshots are mandatory. Capture real running states inside this run's project folder, inspect them yourself, and fix obvious broken/blank/loading/unusable visuals.
- Screenshots must show the actual result, not merely an editor, terminal, loading screen, or blank browser.
- Fix obvious stutter, major loading/resource issues, degraded-over-time performance, broken interactions, and major usability problems encountered during normal use.
- Do not claim completion if the core experience is broken.

Create concise `RESULT.md` with:
Project; Model `ox-alpha`; Harness; Run; Status (completed/partial/failed); launch instructions; screenshot paths; major known issues; duration/turn count if exposed.

A normal README + `RESULT.md` is sufficient unless the project genuinely needs more documentation.

Create an original, fully playable browser-based voxel sandbox game inspired by Minecraft from scratch.

This is NOT a tiny demo, tech demo, static scene, or visual mockup. Build a genuinely playable sandbox/survival game with substantial depth that I can spend meaningful time playing.

The target machine has a powerful discrete GPU. Push visual quality HARD while maintaining good performance.

# PROJECT LOCATION / RUN ISOLATION — CRITICAL

ALL project files MUST live under:

C:\Users\Epic\Documents\ChatGPT\Ox model test

Create a NEW isolated project directory for this run using exactly this naming structure:

`<Project Name> [model:ox-alpha] [<harness-key>] [run:<NN>]`

Use the project name described by this prompt, a short lowercase harness key with no spaces, and a two-digit run number. Start at `01`; if the same project/model/harness folder already exists, reserve the next available number before doing project work. If another parallel run claims it first, increment and retry. Never overwrite, reuse, rename over, or modify another run's folder.

Do NOT use a generic `Minecraft` directory.

Do NOT reuse, modify, delete, reset, clean, move, or overwrite another run's project directory.

If the expected directory already exists and clearly belongs to THIS run and THIS task, inspect it and continue the existing work rather than destroying progress.

Keep source code, dependencies, generated assets, screenshots, caches, tests, saves, and project-specific configuration inside this project's directory wherever practical.

This isolation is intentional because the same challenge may be run simultaneously in multiple execution environments for comparison.

# VISUAL TARGET

Make the game look AMAZING — comparable in atmosphere and visual impact to Minecraft running one of the best modern shader packs.

Include where practical:

- physically convincing sunlight
- dynamic shadows
- beautiful transparent water
- reflections
- atmospheric sky
- volumetric-looking clouds/fog
- bloom
- ambient occlusion
- emissive blocks
- dramatic cave lighting
- day/night cycle
- stars/moon
- sunrise/sunset
- weather
- particles
- vegetation
- high-quality block materials
- strong color grading
- large convincing landscapes
- underwater effects
- distance fog
- dynamic lighting

Use WebGPU when appropriate, with sensible compatibility fallbacks.

Do NOT reduce player-facing visual quality merely because headless automated testing may use software rendering.

If automated/headless rendering is too slow, create a reduced QA/testing graphics mode while preserving High/Ultra modes for real GPUs.

The default experience on a capable GPU should be BEAUTIFUL.

# GAMEPLAY

Recreate the depth and freedom expected from a Minecraft-style sandbox.

Implement as much as reasonably possible, including:

- procedural worlds
- deterministic seeds
- multiple biomes
- mountains
- forests
- plains
- deserts
- oceans/rivers
- caves
- ores
- structures
- chunk loading/unloading
- block breaking
- block placing
- inventory
- hotbar
- crafting
- recipes
- tools
- durability
- health
- hunger
- fall damage
- swimming
- sprinting
- jumping
- mobs
- hostile enemies
- animals
- combat
- drops
- furnaces/smelting
- farming
- storage/chests
- beds
- progression
- multiple material/tool tiers
- torches
- emissive blocks
- basic circuits/automation inspired by redstone
- save/load
- world persistence
- settings
- keybinds
- pause/menu systems

Add additional systems and content when they meaningfully improve the game.

Do not fake systems merely so they can be listed as implemented.

# WORLD

The world should feel expansive and worth exploring.

Use efficient procedural generation and chunk management.

Generate terrain, caves, vegetation, resources, structures and biome transitions coherently.

Optimize expensive systems such as:

- meshing
- lighting
- world generation
- chunk streaming
- collision generation
- physics
- mob AI
- rendering

Do not solve performance problems by simply deleting major features or destroying visual quality.

Profile first and optimize intelligently.

# INPUT / CONTROLS — CRITICAL

Controls must behave exactly as players expect from a modern first-person PC game.

DEFAULT CAMERA:

Mouse RIGHT → camera turns RIGHT.

Mouse LEFT → camera turns LEFT.

Mouse UP → camera looks UP.

Mouse DOWN → camera looks DOWN.

DO NOT ship inverted horizontal or vertical camera controls by default.

If optional inverted-X/inverted-Y settings are implemented, they must be OFF by default.

MOVEMENT:

W = forward relative to camera/player orientation.

S = backward.

A = left.

D = right.

Space = jump.

Shift = sprint.

Mouse movement = look.

Left click = break/attack.

Right click = place/use.

Number keys / mouse wheel = hotbar selection.

Escape = pause and/or safely release pointer lock.

Controls should feel responsive and natural.

Before handoff, briefly play the game and verify that mouse look and WASD move in the intended directions, including after rotating the camera. Also confirm pointer lock/menu transitions do not leave controls stuck. Do not build an exhaustive control test suite unless needed to diagnose a problem.

A visually impressive game with incorrect or inverted controls is NOT complete.

# LOCALHOST / PORT ISOLATION — CRITICAL

Many autonomous coding agents may be running simultaneously on this computer.

Other projects may already have localhost development servers running.

THIS PROJECT MUST NOT INTERFERE WITH THEM.

Before launching any server:

1. Inspect currently listening ports.
2. Choose an AVAILABLE localhost port specifically for this project.
3. Prefer keeping that port consistent for future runs when possible.
4. Record the selected port somewhere inside this project's workspace.

DO NOT assume these are free:

3000
3001
4000
5000
5173
5174
8000
8080
8888

Check first.

If your desired port is occupied:

DO NOT kill the process.

DO NOT restart it.

DO NOT modify it.

DO NOT take over its port.

Choose another available port.

Bind development servers to:

127.0.0.1 / localhost

unless there is a genuine technical requirement otherwise.

DO NOT:

- kill unrelated Node processes
- kill unrelated Python processes
- stop unrelated development servers
- stop unrelated Docker containers
- modify another project's files
- modify another project's configuration
- reuse another agent's server
- globally clean processes because of a conflict
- use broad taskkill/pkill commands against shared runtimes

Track subprocesses belonging to THIS project and only clean up processes you created.

Treat every other localhost service as an unrelated production workload.

OTHER AGENTS ARE WORKING SIMULTANEOUSLY.

DO NOT FIGHT THEM OVER PORTS.

# PROJECT ISOLATION

Keep all source code, generated assets, caches, screenshots, tests and project-specific configuration within this project's workspace wherever practical.

Do not modify unrelated repositories.

Do not make destructive host-level changes.

Install dependencies project-locally when practical.

# AUTONOMY

Work autonomously.

Do not stop at a plan.

Do not ask me to implement routine intermediate steps.

Choose appropriate technologies, libraries, architecture and implementation strategies yourself.

You may:

- create/edit project files
- install reasonable project-local dependencies
- run builds
- run tests
- launch this project's localhost server
- use headless browsers
- use browser automation
- capture screenshots
- inspect rendered output
- profile performance
- create test worlds
- generate assets
- restart THIS project's services

Do not make destructive changes outside this project's workspace.

If one approach fails, diagnose WHY and attempt another reasonable solution.

# WORK IN PASSES

Build iteratively, but keep the process lightweight.

Suggested flow:

1. Core world + rendering
2. Player + sandbox mechanics
3. Survival/progression/content
4. Persistence + performance
5. Final verification + visual polish

Combine or reorder these as useful. Do not create separate QA/regression passes unless problems actually require them.

# FINAL VERIFICATION — REQUIRED

Before handing the game to me, actually play it long enough to confirm the core experience works. At minimum verify movement/camera direction, breaking and placing blocks, inventory/crafting, basic survival interaction, and save/reload. Fix any blocking or obviously broken behavior you encounter.

Screenshots are mandatory. Capture at least 2 real in-game screenshots from representative gameplay states, inspect the actual pixels, and fix obvious visual problems before handoff. More screenshots/testing are welcome when useful, but do not turn QA into an exhaustive checklist unless the game exposes a real issue that needs deeper investigation.

If headless rendering is slow, lower only the QA graphics settings; preserve the player-facing High/Ultra experience.

# PERFORMANCE

This game should run smoothly on capable desktop hardware.

Profile before simplifying.

Optimize hot paths in:

- chunk generation
- voxel meshing
- lighting
- collision
- physics
- AI
- draw calls
- material switching
- memory allocation
- save/load
- world streaming

Use techniques such as workers/background processing, meshing optimization, frustum culling, instancing, sensible chunk scheduling and caching where appropriate.

Avoid long main-thread stalls during exploration.

Graphics settings should allow sensible scalability.

ULTRA should prioritize beauty.

Lower settings may prioritize weaker hardware.

# AUDIO / GAME FEEL

Add appropriate original or safely usable audio where practical:

- footsteps
- block interactions
- ambience
- weather
- water
- caves
- mobs
- combat
- UI feedback

Improve responsiveness and game feel with appropriate animations, particles and feedback.

# DO NOT FAKE COMPLETION

Do NOT declare success merely because:

- dependencies installed
- the project compiles
- the server starts
- the page loads
- WebGL/WebGPU initializes
- terrain renders
- the player moves
- one screenshot looks good
- automated tests partially pass

Those are milestones.

They are NOT completion.

# DEFINITION OF DONE

The project is complete when I can open the provided localhost URL and experience a substantial, polished, beautiful, genuinely playable voxel sandbox.

I should be able to:

EXPLORE
→ SURVIVE
→ MINE
→ CRAFT
→ BUILD
→ FIGHT
→ PROGRESS
→ SAVE
→ RETURN
→ CONTINUE.

Controls must be correct.

World generation must work.

Performance must be reasonable.

Important gameplay systems must work together.

The game must visually hold up under actual inspection.

At completion, provide:

- exact project directory
- run identifier name
- localhost URL and selected port
- controls
- major implemented systems
- graphics modes
- performance observations
- tests performed
- visual QA performed
- known limitations, if any

Leave the localhost build in a state where I can immediately open and play it.

You are working on a powerful PC now.

Do not build the minimum Minecraft clone.

Build the voxel sandbox that demonstrates what you can actually do when given autonomy, GPU resources, testing tools and time.

May the chunks load.

May the shaders compile.

May the controls NOT invert.

May the execution environments remain in their own fucking folders.

May the tokens flow.

Build a substantial open-world game that I can genuinely PLAY.

The target PC has a powerful discrete GPU. Push browser graphics HARD while maintaining good performance.

Do not copy Rockstar's proprietary code, maps, characters, logos, story, music or assets. Create an original city, characters, identity and content.

Create a dense open-world city where I can freely:

- explore on foot
- drive vehicles
- steal/enter/exit vehicles
- interact with NPCs
- fight
- use weapons
- commit crimes
- attract police attention
- escape police
- complete missions
- earn/spend money
- discover activities
- explore interesting locations

The world should feel alive rather than like an empty graphics demo.

# CITY

Build an original, substantial city with:

- downtown
- skyscrapers
- neighborhoods
- highways
- intersections
- alleys
- parking areas
- stores
- industrial areas
- parks
- beaches/waterfront where appropriate
- landmarks
- enterable locations where practical
- traffic lights
- street lights
- sidewalks
- road markings
- props
- vegetation
- pedestrians
- traffic

Use procedural/systemic generation where useful, but avoid obvious repetitive city-grid syndrome.

Create recognizable districts with different visual identities.

The city should reward exploration.

# GRAPHICS — PUSH HARD

Target a high-end modern browser-game presentation.

Implement where appropriate:

- PBR materials
- physically convincing sunlight
- dynamic shadows
- reflections
- high-quality water
- atmospheric scattering
- beautiful sky
- sunrise/sunset
- day/night cycle
- nighttime city lighting
- emissive windows/signage
- weather
- rain
- wet-road reflections
- fog
- bloom
- ambient occlusion
- particles
- vehicle lights
- headlights
- brake lights
- street lights
- strong color grading
- detailed environments
- convincing distance rendering

Use WebGPU where beneficial with appropriate fallback strategies.

The target machine has a REAL discrete GPU.

DO NOT downgrade the actual player experience merely because automated/headless testing uses SwiftShader or another software renderer.

If headless testing cannot render Ultra efficiently, implement a dedicated QA graphics mode.

QA MODE may be lightweight.

ULTRA MODE should make the GPU WORK.

# PLAYER

Implement a polished third-person controller.

Include:

- walking
- running
- sprinting
- jumping
- camera orbit
- aiming
- combat
- entering/exiting vehicles
- interactions
- health
- death/respawn

Movement and animation should feel responsive.

Avoid placeholder capsule-character quality in the finished experience.

Create or generate an original stylized player character appropriate for the game.

# VEHICLES

Vehicles are a major feature.

Implement:

- multiple vehicle types
- acceleration
- braking
- reversing
- steering
- handbrake
- collisions
- suspension-like behavior where practical
- vehicle damage
- entering/exiting
- traffic AI
- parked vehicles
- headlights
- brake lights
- different handling characteristics

Driving should be FUN, not merely functional.

# NPCs / WORLD SIMULATION

Create pedestrians that make the city feel populated.

NPCs should have behaviors such as:

- walking
- wandering
- crossing streets
- reacting to player actions
- fleeing danger
- reacting to collisions
- reacting to weapons/crime
- interacting with world locations

Traffic should navigate roads and respond reasonably to intersections, obstacles and other vehicles.

# CRIME / POLICE

Implement a real wanted system.

Crimes should increase police attention.

Include multiple escalation levels.

Police should:

- detect crimes
- pursue the player
- navigate streets
- use vehicles where appropriate
- search for the player
- escalate response
- lose track of the player under sensible conditions

Escaping a serious pursuit should feel like gameplay, not waiting for a timer.

# COMBAT

Implement satisfying combat.

Include where appropriate:

- melee
- firearms
- aiming
- projectiles/hitscan
- ammunition
- damage
- NPC reactions
- cover-aware behavior if practical
- police combat
- weapon switching

Provide clear visual/audio feedback.

# MISSIONS / ACTIVITIES

Create actual playable content.

Implement several missions demonstrating different systems, such as:

- driving
- chase
- delivery
- escape
- exploration
- combat
- timed challenge

Add optional activities where practical.

Do not merely create mission markers with placeholder text.

# WORLD SYSTEMS

Include:

- money
- health
- wanted level
- minimap
- objective system
- save/load
- settings
- graphics options
- audio options
- control options
- pause menu
- persistence

Add additional systems when they improve the experience.

# INPUT / CONTROLS — CRITICAL

CONTROLS MUST NOT BE INVERTED.

Third-person camera:

Mouse RIGHT → camera rotates RIGHT.
Mouse LEFT → camera rotates LEFT.
Mouse UP → camera looks UP.
Mouse DOWN → camera looks DOWN.

Inverted X/Y options may exist but MUST be OFF by default.

ON FOOT:

W = forward
S = backward
A = left
D = right
Mouse = camera
Shift = sprint
Space = jump
Left click = attack/fire
Right click = aim where appropriate
E = interact / enter vehicle
Escape = pause/release pointer

VEHICLES:

W = accelerate
S = brake/reverse
A = steer LEFT
D = steer RIGHT
Space = handbrake where appropriate
E = exit vehicle

Steering MUST NOT be reversed.

Camera-relative movement must remain correct after camera rotation.

Before handoff, briefly verify the resulting camera/player movement and vehicle steering so mouse/WASD directions are correct and not inverted. Include at least one check after camera rotation and one driving check. Do not require a large dedicated input regression suite unless a problem appears.

A beautiful game with backwards controls is NOT complete.

# LOCALHOST / PORT ISOLATION — CRITICAL

Many autonomous agents and execution environments may be working simultaneously on this computer.

Before starting a server:

1. Inspect currently listening ports.
2. Select an AVAILABLE localhost port for THIS GTA project.
3. Record it inside the project.
4. Reuse it later when available.
5. If occupied later, choose another free port.

DO NOT assume common development ports are available.

If a port is occupied:

DO NOT kill its process.
DO NOT restart it.
DO NOT steal it.
DO NOT modify it.

Pick another port.

Bind to:

127.0.0.1 / localhost

unless genuinely necessary otherwise.

NEVER broadly kill Node, Python, browser, Docker or development processes.

Do NOT use broad taskkill/pkill commands.

Only terminate processes positively identified as belonging to THIS project.

Do not interfere with:

- Minecraft
- EpicVM
- other games
- other agent sessions
- other execution environments
- unrelated localhost services

OTHER AGENTS ARE WORKING.

DO NOT START A PORT WAR.

# AUTONOMY

Work autonomously.

Do not stop at a plan.

Choose architecture and technologies yourself.

You may:

- create/edit project files
- install project-local dependencies
- build
- test
- run this project's server
- use browser automation
- use headless browsers
- capture screenshots
- inspect rendered pixels
- generate original assets
- profile performance
- create automated gameplay tests

Do not make destructive changes outside this project's directory.

If something fails, diagnose it and continue toward the goal.

# WORK IN PASSES

Build iteratively without turning every subsystem into its own mandatory test phase.

Suggested flow:

1. City + rendering
2. Player + vehicles
3. NPCs + combat + police
4. Missions/world systems + persistence
5. Performance + final polish/verification

Combine or reorder passes as useful. Add deeper regression testing only when needed.

# FINAL VERIFICATION — REQUIRED

Before handoff, actually play a representative slice of the game and confirm the core loop works: move around, enter/drive/exit a vehicle, interact or fight, trigger the wanted/police system, and progress a mission or activity. Confirm controls are not inverted and fix blocking bugs you encounter.

Screenshots are mandatory. Capture at least 2 real in-game screenshots showing representative gameplay, inspect the pixels, and fix obvious visual problems before handoff. Extra testing is encouraged when useful, but an exhaustive automated city-wide regression suite is not required.

# PERFORMANCE

Profile before simplifying.

Optimize:

- draw calls
- geometry
- materials
- traffic
- NPC AI
- physics
- shadows
- reflections
- world streaming
- memory
- post-processing

Use LOD, instancing, culling, streaming and other appropriate techniques.

Do not make the city empty merely to increase FPS.

Provide scalable graphics presets.

Ultra should prioritize visual quality on capable hardware.

# DO NOT FAKE COMPLETION

The game is NOT complete because:

- a city renders
- driving works
- NPCs spawn
- weapons fire
- police appear
- the server runs
- one screenshot looks good

Those are milestones.

# DEFINITION OF DONE

I should be able to open the localhost URL and genuinely PLAY an original browser open-world action game.

I should be able to:

EXPLORE
→ WALK
→ DRIVE
→ INTERACT
→ COMMIT CRIMES
→ GET CHASED
→ FIGHT
→ COMPLETE MISSIONS
→ SAVE
→ RETURN
→ CONTINUE.

The city must look good.

Driving must feel good.

Controls must be correct.

NPCs and traffic must make the city feel alive.

Police/wanted gameplay must genuinely function.

Performance must be reasonable.

At completion report:

- exact project directory
- run identifier
- localhost URL/port
- controls
- implemented systems
- missions/content
- graphics modes
- performance observations
- gameplay tests
- visual QA
- known limitations

Leave the localhost build running or otherwise immediately runnable for me to play.

Do not build another empty browser city demo.

Build the open-world game that makes me ask how the hell this came out of one prompt.

May the towers remain solid.

May the streets stay populated.

May the steering NOT invert.

May the ports remain peaceful.

May the tokens flow.

BENCHMARK EXECUTION CONTRACT

Run identity / isolation
- Model: `ox-alpha`.
- All project files must live under `C:\Users\Epic\Documents\ChatGPT\Ox model test`.
- Required folder: `<Project Name> [model:ox-alpha] [<harness-key>] [run:<NN>]`.
- Use a short lowercase harness key. Start at `run:01`; if that project/model/harness already exists, atomically claim the next available two-digit run number.
- Never overwrite, reuse, rename over, or modify another run's folder. Keep project dependencies/artifacts inside this run folder where practical.

Browser-only + parallel testing
- Finished project must run in a standard modern browser. Local dev servers are fine; Electron/Tauri/native runtimes are not substitutes.
- Assume many runs test simultaneously. Use a unique free localhost port, isolated browser profile/context, and run-scoped temp/cache/download/trace/screenshot artifacts.
- Never hijack, navigate, close, or kill unrelated browser tabs/processes/servers, and never kill something merely to free a port.
- Track/clean up only resources created by this run. Prefer headless testing unless visible interaction is genuinely required.

- Keep critical runtime assets/dependencies local or bundled when practical so the finished project does not unnecessarily depend on fragile third-party CDNs/APIs just to boot.
- Handle browser user-gesture restrictions correctly for features such as audio, fullscreen, pointer lock, clipboard, autoplay, or similar browser-gated capabilities; provide a clear user action instead of silently failing.
- If the project has non-obvious controls or shortcuts, expose them clearly in the experience through a controls/help overlay, onboarding hint, pause/menu screen, or similarly discoverable UI.

Execution efficiency
- Prefer the shortest direct implementation path that satisfies the task; investigate only enough to unblock building.
- Batch related checks when practical. Use bounded retries and switch strategy when an approach repeatedly fails.
- Preserve working progress. Finish the core vertical slice before extras.
- Avoid scope creep, prolonged architecture archaeology, over-debugging non-blockers, and stalling on optional services/assets; use sensible local/generated/mock fallbacks when useful.
- Verify real functionality, but do not run huge regression/stress/profiling suites unless a discovered issue warrants them.

Quality + performance
- Build a polished, coherent finished experience, not a checklist demo.
- Prioritize usability, visual quality, interaction feel, responsive feedback, consistent styling, and sensible design decisions.
- Avoid unfinished/debug/placeholder-looking final states when better treatment materially improves the result.
- Implement important behavior for real rather than faking it for screenshots. Keep code organized without overengineering.
- Keep runtime smooth/resource-conscious: avoid unbounded objects/effects/listeners/workers/requests, unnecessary per-frame work, runaway CPU/GPU/memory use, oversized assets, and performance that degrades over time.
- Reuse/pool/batch/cull/pause/clean up work when useful. Optimize the actual experience, not synthetic numbers, and do not sacrifice meaningful quality just to chase metrics.

Optional capabilities
- You may use any additional input modalities, inspection capabilities, or environment-provided tools when genuinely useful. Their use is optional; do not create extra work simply because they exist.

OPTIONAL CAPABILITY — ISOLATED E2E TESTING (contested-machine browser protocol)
If this run does any browser automation / E2E testing / screenshots and
{{E2E_ISOLATION_SKILL_PATH}} is not UNAVAILABLE, read and follow that SKILL.md
before your first browser/playwright step. Core rules it enforces: prefer
deterministic non-browser tests; ONE tab maximum (a second client is a raw
in-page WebSocket or node script, never a second tab); stamp every tab
(window.__TID) and re-assert stamp+URL before EVERY browser tool call;
abandon silently any tab showing someone else's page; keep trigger→assert
steps atomic under UI fade/expiry windows; clean up only process PIDs you
recorded spawning — never name-filter sweeps. Skill artifacts stay inside
this run's project folder. If the path is UNAVAILABLE, proceed using the
isolation rules above.

IMAGE GENERATION — USE THIS SKILL, NOTHING ELSE
If image generation/editing would genuinely help, use only:
`C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs`
No API keys or browser automation for image generation.

Rules:
- Node 18+; always pass `-o`; parse stdout exactly.
- Do not wrap/parallelize the script or create sleep-loop retry logic; keep `--delay-ms >= 1500`.
- Plus capacity is limited (~50 images/3h), so wait instead of retry-spamming limits.
- On 401, tell the user to run `codex login`.
- Sizes: `1024x1024|1024x1536|1536x1024`; quality: `low|medium|high`.

Single:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" -o out.png "PROMPT"`
Successful stdout = exactly one line, the absolute PNG path.

Batch:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" --n 10 --quality low -o sheet.png "PROMPT"`
Outputs `sheet-1.png`...`sheet-10.png`; exit `0` all ok / `2` partial / `1` fail; logs on stderr.

Edit:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" --ref input.png -o out.png "INSTRUCTION"`

For >3 images/background work:
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue add [-o x.png] "PROMPT"`
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue run --detach`
`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue status --json`
Poll about every 20s until `pending==0 && running==0`.
Use `queue list --json` for `.path`/`.error`; retry failed items with `queue run --retry-failed`.

CONDITIONAL MULTIPLAYER BUILD CONTRACT v2
Applies only if multiplayer is included. Epic handles deployment; you build only.
- Produce ONE self-contained static build folder suitable for `OxAlpha/<Project>/<Harness>/`.
- Do NOT deploy, push, SSH, edit compose files, touch Traefik, or run anything on the server.
- Multiplayer build folder: `<Project>-<Harness>` (Hermes harness unless told otherwise).
- Entry: root `index.html`, or `public/index.html` with that structure intact.
- `arcade.json` beside entry:
  `{"title":"<Human Name>","description":"<one line>","multiplayer":{"endpoint":"/ws/<project-slug>"}}`
- Slug must be lowercase `[a-z0-9-]` and match the `server.mjs` route exactly.

Optional backend:
- If needed, add ONE `server.mjs` beside entry: ESM, Node builtins only, no npm packages, no `listen()`, no spawned server.
- Platform loads a default export with optional `maxSockets`, optional `tickMs`, and `create(ctx)` returning `open`, `message`, `close`, optional `tick`, optional `stop`.
- `ws` provides `{ id, send(obj|string), close(code), query(URLSearchParams), ip }`.
- State is memory-only; clients reconnect/rejoin after restart. Keep handlers deterministic/fast. If offline-only, omit `server.mjs`.

Client netcode:
- Same-origin/subpath-safe only:
  `const url=(location.protocol==="https:"?"wss://":"ws://")+location.host+"/ws/<project-slug>";`
- Never hardcode domains/ports/`ws://localhost` or root-absolute asset/worker/importScripts paths.
- Auto-reconnect with backoff and graceful disconnected UI.
- Netcode belongs in normal source dirs.
- Game must still boot pure-static if backend is down, and from `file://` or a dumb static server.

Multiplayer handoff: state Project, Harness, entry path, endpoint, and message protocol/event payloads.

FINAL VERIFICATION / HANDOFF
- Launch the real project in a browser and exercise the core experience enough to catch obvious blockers.
- Screenshots are mandatory. Capture real running states inside this run's project folder, inspect them yourself, and fix obvious broken/blank/loading/unusable visuals.
- Screenshots must show the actual result, not merely an editor, terminal, loading screen, or blank browser.
- Fix obvious stutter, major loading/resource issues, degraded-over-time performance, broken interactions, and major usability problems encountered during normal use.
- Do not claim completion if the core experience is broken.

Create concise `RESULT.md` with:
Project; Model `ox-alpha`; Harness; Run; Status (completed/partial/failed); launch instructions; screenshot paths; major known issues; duration/turn count if exposed.

A normal README + `RESULT.md` is sufficient unless the project genuinely needs more documentation.

Create from scratch an original, fully playable browser-based survival horror game inspired by the tension, surveillance gameplay, atmosphere and animatronic horror of Five Nights at Freddy's.

This is NOT a tiny FNAF clone, static room, jumpscare demo, visual mockup or collection of scripted scenes.

Build a substantial, polished horror game with original characters, environments, lore and gameplay.

Do NOT copy proprietary FNAF characters, models, maps, sounds, music, logos, story or assets.

Create an ORIGINAL animatronic horror experience.

The target PC has a powerful discrete GPU. Push browser graphics, lighting, animation and atmosphere HARD.

# PROJECT LOCATION / RUN ISOLATION — CRITICAL

ALL project files MUST live under:

C:\Users\Epic\Documents\ChatGPT\Ox model test

Create a NEW isolated project directory for this run using exactly this naming structure:

`<Project Name> [model:ox-alpha] [<harness-key>] [run:<NN>]`

Use the project name described by this prompt, a short lowercase harness key with no spaces, and a two-digit run number. Start at `01`; if the same project/model/harness folder already exists, reserve the next available number before doing project work. If another parallel run claims it first, increment and retry. Never overwrite, reuse, rename over, or modify another run's folder.

Do NOT use a generic `FNAF` directory.

Do NOT reuse, modify, delete, reset, clean, move, or overwrite another run's project directory.

If the expected directory already exists and clearly belongs to THIS run and THIS task, inspect it and continue the existing work rather than destroying progress.

Keep source code, dependencies, generated assets, screenshots, caches, tests, saves, and project-specific configuration inside this project's directory wherever practical.

This isolation is intentional because the same challenge may be run simultaneously in multiple execution environments for comparison.

# CORE EXPERIENCE

Create a tense nighttime survival experience built around surveillance, resource management, environmental awareness and intelligent animatronic threats.

The player should need to:

- monitor security cameras
- track animatronics
- listen for audio cues
- manage limited resources
- operate defensive systems
- make strategic decisions
- survive increasingly difficult nights
- discover hidden story/lore
- learn enemy behaviors

Do NOT make success depend purely on random jumpscares.

The player should gradually understand each threat and develop strategies.

# ORIGINAL LOCATION

Create an original entertainment venue with a distinctive identity.

Include areas such as:

- security office
- performance area
- dining/entertainment spaces
- backstage
- maintenance
- hallways
- storage
- staff areas
- kitchen
- entrances
- hidden areas
- ventilation/service routes where appropriate

Create a coherent layout that matters to gameplay.

Security cameras should correspond to actual locations.

# ORIGINAL ANIMATRONICS

Create multiple ORIGINAL animatronic characters.

Each should have:

- recognizable silhouette
- unique personality/theme
- distinct movement behavior
- unique threat mechanics
- readable tells
- different counter-strategy
- animations
- sounds
- jumpscare behavior

Do not simply recolor the same model repeatedly.

Their designs should be memorable and genuinely unsettling.

# 3D ASSET QUALITY

Where useful, use programmatic/headless 3D asset-generation workflows such as Blender scripting to create ORIGINAL game assets.

If Blender is available, you may use it headlessly through CLI/Python.

For important models:

CREATE
→ RENDER
→ CAPTURE IMAGE
→ INSPECT
→ IDENTIFY PROBLEMS
→ MODIFY
→ RENDER AGAIN.

Preserve editable source files such as `.blend` where practical.

Important animatronics should have proper:

- geometry
- materials
- rigging
- joints
- animation
- eyes
- mouth/jaw mechanisms
- recognizable silhouettes

Avoid finished-game characters that look like placeholder cubes/capsules.

# GRAPHICS / HORROR PRESENTATION

Push visual quality HARD.

Implement where appropriate:

- PBR materials
- dynamic shadows
- flickering lights
- volumetric-looking fog
- darkness
- bloom used carefully
- reflections
- grime
- worn materials
- emissive signage
- CRT/security-camera effects
- camera noise
- signal interference
- atmospheric particles
- dramatic contrast
- animated monitors
- emergency lighting
- environmental storytelling
- high-quality post-processing

Darkness must remain readable enough for gameplay.

Do not simply crush the entire screen to black.

Use lighting deliberately to create tension.

# SECURITY CAMERA SYSTEM

Build a genuine camera network.

The player should be able to:

- open camera interface
- switch cameras
- identify locations
- observe animatronics
- track movement
- encounter interference
- use cameras strategically

Animatronics should actually move between meaningful world states/locations.

Do not fake the entire system with unrelated prerecorded images.

Camera feeds should reflect the game's actual state where practical.

# ANIMATRONIC AI

Create real enemy behavior.

Animatronics should:

- progress through locations
- react to player behavior
- have distinct movement logic
- become more dangerous over time
- interact with cameras/doors/defenses
- produce readable audio/visual clues
- reach the player if defenses fail

Avoid pure random teleportation unless it is intentionally part of a specific character's mechanic.

Difficulty should increase across nights.

# OFFICE / DEFENSE SYSTEMS

Give the player meaningful tools.

Examples:

- doors
- lights
- camera system
- ventilation
- audio distractions
- emergency systems
- motion detection
- limited power
- batteries
- breakers
- temporary defenses

Balance these systems so the player cannot simply leave everything enabled.

# RESOURCE MANAGEMENT

Implement meaningful resource pressure.

For example:

POWER
→ cameras consume power
→ lights consume power
→ doors consume power
→ defenses consume power
→ careless use causes failure.

Make resource usage understandable and strategically interesting rather than arbitrary.

# AUDIO — EXTREMELY IMPORTANT

Horror depends heavily on sound.

Create/use appropriate original or safely usable audio for:

- footsteps
- mechanical movement
- distant impacts
- servos
- breathing/ambient noise
- ventilation
- electrical hum
- camera switching
- static
- doors
- warning systems
- jumpscares
- environmental ambience

Use positional/spatial audio where useful.

Important threats should sometimes be detectable through SOUND before sight.

# NIGHTS / PROGRESSION

Create multiple playable nights or equivalent stages.

Each should introduce or escalate mechanics.

Example progression:

Night 1 — learn basic surveillance.
Night 2 — additional threat.
Night 3 — resource pressure increases.
Night 4 — behaviors combine.
Night 5 — full challenge.

Add additional/endgame content if practical.

Include difficulty progression rather than simply increasing enemy speed.

# STORY / LORE

Create original environmental storytelling.

Use things such as:

- recordings
- notes
- posters
- hidden rooms
- camera anomalies
- maintenance logs
- environmental clues
- secret interactions

Do not dump the entire story through giant text walls.

Let players discover it.

# JUMPSCARES

Jumpscares should be earned through gameplay failure.

Create high-quality animations, lighting and sound.

Do not rely on cheap full-screen image flashes.

Use actual animated characters where practical.

# INPUT / CONTROLS — CRITICAL

CONTROLS MUST NOT BE INVERTED.

If the player can freely look around:

Mouse RIGHT → view RIGHT.
Mouse LEFT → view LEFT.
Mouse UP → look UP.
Mouse DOWN → look DOWN.

Inverted X/Y options may exist but MUST be OFF by default.

For any free movement:

W = forward
S = backward
A = left
D = right

Interaction controls must behave naturally and consistently.

Camera-map controls must correspond to the locations they claim to show.

Before handoff, briefly play and verify that camera/look movement and interactions produce the intended in-game result and are not inverted. Confirm camera-map interactions correspond to the correct locations. Deeper input testing is optional unless a bug appears.

A beautiful horror game with backwards controls is NOT complete.

# HEADLESS AUTOMATION — CRITICAL

ALL automated browser testing MUST run HEADLESS.

Do NOT:

- open visible browser windows
- control the user's personal browser
- navigate the user's browser
- close the user's browser
- steal keyboard focus
- steal mouse focus
- move the user's cursor
- type into unrelated applications
- use desktop GUI automation against the user's active desktop
- interfere with the user's normal PC usage

Use isolated headless browser instances for automated testing and screenshots.

The user must remain able to use the computer normally while you work.

If a test cannot safely run headlessly, find another automated testing strategy rather than hijacking the user's desktop.

# LOCALHOST / PORT ISOLATION — CRITICAL

Other autonomous agents are running simultaneously.

Before launching any server:

1. Inspect listening ports.
2. Choose an AVAILABLE localhost port specifically for THIS project.
3. Record the selected port inside this project.
4. Reuse it later when available.
5. If occupied, choose another free port.

DO NOT assume common ports are free.

If a port is occupied:

DO NOT kill its process.
DO NOT restart it.
DO NOT modify it.
DO NOT steal the port.

Choose another port.

Bind to:

127.0.0.1 / localhost

unless genuinely necessary otherwise.

NEVER broadly kill Node, Python, browser, Docker or development processes.

Do not use broad taskkill/pkill commands.

Only terminate processes positively identified as belonging to THIS project.

Do not interfere with:

- Minecraft
- GTA
- EpicVM
- other games
- other agent sessions
- other agent sessions
- other execution environments
- unrelated localhost services

OTHER AGENTS ARE WORKING.

DO NOT START A PORT WAR.

# AUTONOMY

Work autonomously.

Do not stop at a plan.

Choose architecture, technologies and implementation strategies yourself.

You may:

- create/edit project files
- install project-local dependencies
- use headless Blender if available
- generate original assets
- run builds
- run tests
- launch this project's localhost server
- use HEADLESS browser automation
- capture screenshots
- inspect rendered pixels
- profile performance
- create automated gameplay tests

Do not make destructive changes outside this project's directory.

If something fails, diagnose it and continue.

# WORK IN PASSES

Build iteratively and keep validation focused on the playable experience.

Suggested flow:

1. Location + animatronics
2. Cameras + AI + defense systems
3. Nights/progression + audio/horror presentation
4. Graphics + performance
5. Final verification + polish

Do not create separate full-regression passes unless a real bug or risky change makes them necessary.

# FINAL VERIFICATION — REQUIRED

Before handoff, actually play enough of the horror loop to verify the security cameras, animatronic movement/AI, defenses, resource use, win/lose behavior, and progression are functioning together. Fix blockers and obvious gameplay failures.

Screenshots are mandatory. Capture at least 2 real screenshots from representative states such as the office/camera view and a tense animatronic encounter, inspect the pixels, and fix obvious visual issues before handoff. Additional tests are optional unless needed to diagnose a problem.

# PERFORMANCE

Profile before simplifying.

Optimize:

- rendering
- shadows
- camera feeds
- animation
- AI
- post-processing
- memory
- asset loading

Use graphics presets where appropriate.

QA mode may reduce rendering complexity for headless testing.

High/Ultra should preserve the intended visual experience for real GPUs.

# DO NOT FAKE COMPLETION

The game is NOT complete because:

- the office renders
- cameras switch
- an animatronic moves
- a jumpscare works
- the server starts
- one night technically finishes
- one screenshot looks good

Those are milestones.

# DEFINITION OF DONE

I should be able to open the localhost URL and play a polished original animatronic survival-horror game.

I should be able to:

MONITOR
→ LISTEN
→ REASON
→ MANAGE RESOURCES
→ DEFEND
→ SURVIVE
→ PROGRESS
→ DISCOVER SECRETS.

Animatronics must genuinely threaten me.

Camera gameplay must matter.

Audio must matter.

Resource management must matter.

Controls must be correct.

Create from scratch an original, fully playable browser-based third-person battle royale game inspired by the building, combat, movement, destruction and fast-paced sandbox gameplay of Fortnite.

This is NOT a tiny clone, shooting demo, static island, tech demo or fake battle royale.

Build a substantial battle royale game that I can genuinely PLAY.

Do NOT copy Epic Games' proprietary code, characters, skins, maps, logos, music, story or assets. Create an ORIGINAL identity, island, characters, weapons, environments and content.

The target PC has a powerful discrete GPU. Push browser graphics HARD while maintaining excellent responsiveness.

C:\Users\Epic\Documents\ChatGPT\Ox model test

LOBBY
→ MATCH START
→ DROP
→ LAND
→ LOOT
→ GATHER MATERIALS
→ FIGHT
→ BUILD
→ SURVIVE STORM
→ ELIMINATE OPPONENTS
→ FINAL CIRCLE
→ VICTORY / DEFEAT
→ PLAY AGAIN.

- multiple named locations
- towns
- buildings
- forests
- hills
- water
- roads
- bridges
- landmarks
- interiors
- loot locations
- open combat spaces
- dense combat spaces
- traversal routes
- environmental cover

Locations should have distinct visual identities.

Avoid an empty procedural landscape.

The map should encourage exploration, rotations and different combat strategies.

Include:

- pre-match state/lobby where useful
- aerial transport or equivalent original deployment system
- player-controlled drop
- freefall
- gliding/parachuting
- landing
- bots/opponents dropping across the island

Opponents must NOT all spawn directly on the ground before the player.

The opening should visually communicate that a battle royale match is beginning.

Include:

- walking
- running
- sprinting
- jumping
- crouching
- aiming
- shooting
- reloading
- weapon switching
- harvesting
- building
- editing
- interacting
- swimming where appropriate
- gliding
- taking damage
- healing
- death/spectating/end-state

Movement should feel fast, responsive and enjoyable.

Add additional modern traversal such as sliding, mantling or similar systems where useful.

Implement:

- multiple weapon classes
- different damage values
- fire rates
- recoil
- spread
- magazines
- reloads
- ammunition
- weapon switching
- aiming
- hit detection
- head/body damage differences where appropriate
- health
- shields
- elimination
- hit feedback
- damage indicators
- muzzle effects
- impact effects

Create original weapons.

Include categories such as:

- assault weapon
- shotgun
- SMG
- precision/sniper weapon
- explosive or special weapon

Combat should feel responsive and satisfying.

# LOOT

Create a meaningful loot system.

Include:

- weapons
- ammunition
- healing
- shields
- utility items
- building resources
- rarity tiers where appropriate

Distribute loot throughout buildings and locations.

Add containers/chests or an original equivalent.

Loot should create meaningful decisions.

Implement a fast building system inspired by battle royale construction mechanics.

Allow players to build:

- walls
- floors
- ramps
- roofs/cones where practical

Building should:

- snap predictably
- preview placement
- consume resources
- respect collision
- support rapid placement
- be destructible

Allow structures to take damage and break.

# EDITING

Implement structure editing where practical.

Players should be able to modify owned structures to create useful openings or alternate shapes.

Editing must be responsive enough to use during combat.

# HARVESTING / DESTRUCTION

Allow players to gather materials from the environment.

Include multiple resource types where useful.

Player harvesting should:

- damage objects
- provide feedback
- grant materials
- eventually destroy harvestable objects

World destruction should visually communicate damage.

Buildings/props should react appropriately where feasible.

Include:

- initial safe zone
- visible storm boundary
- multiple shrinking phases
- map indicator
- countdown
- storm damage
- increasingly small final circles

The storm must actually influence rotations and fights.

Bots should understand and react to the safe zone.

Bots should:

- drop onto the island
- loot
- navigate
- move toward safe zones
- detect enemies
- fight
- use different weapons
- seek cover
- heal where appropriate
- react to the storm
- eliminate each other
- pursue or disengage intelligently

Avoid opponents that merely stand still and shoot.

Bots should continue simulating the match even when far from the player using appropriate lower-cost simulation.

The battle royale must actually progress.

Bots should fight one another.

Player count should decrease.

Storm phases should progress.

The final surviving participant should win.

Display remaining-player count.

A victory must be genuinely achievable.

Target a polished stylized AAA-inspired browser presentation.

Implement where appropriate:

- high-quality stylized materials
- dynamic sunlight
- dynamic shadows
- atmospheric sky
- beautiful clouds
- water
- reflections
- ambient occlusion
- bloom used carefully
- fog
- vegetation
- wind
- particles
- weather
- day/time atmosphere
- detailed locations
- weapon effects
- destruction effects
- storm effects
- strong color grading
- polished animation
- high-quality UI

Use WebGPU where beneficial with appropriate compatibility fallbacks.

DO NOT reduce player-facing graphics merely because headless automated testing uses software rendering.

Create a dedicated reduced-quality QA mode when necessary.

QA mode may be lightweight.

HIGH/ULTRA must preserve the intended visual experience for a real discrete GPU.

Ultra should make the GPU earn its electricity.

Create original assets and visual identity.

Where useful, use procedural generation or headless 3D asset workflows.

If Blender is available, you may automate it headlessly using CLI/Python.

Do not depend primarily on ripped/downloaded proprietary game assets.

# INPUT / CONTROLS — EXTREMELY CRITICAL

THE PREVIOUS EXPERIMENT HAD INVERTED CONTROLS.

DO NOT REPEAT THIS.

DEFAULT CAMERA MUST BE:

Mouse RIGHT → camera rotates RIGHT.
Mouse LEFT → camera rotates LEFT.
Mouse UP → camera looks UP.
Mouse DOWN → camera looks DOWN.

DO NOT ship inverted X or Y controls by default.

If invert-X/invert-Y settings exist, BOTH MUST DEFAULT TO OFF.

PLAYER:

W = move forward relative to intended camera/player direction.
S = backward.
A = LEFT.
D = RIGHT.
Space = jump.
Shift = sprint.
Ctrl/C = crouch where appropriate.
Mouse = camera.
Left click = fire/use primary action.
Right click = aim.
R = reload.
E = interact.
Number keys / mouse wheel = weapon/item selection.

Building controls should be intuitive and configurable.

Escape = pause/release pointer where appropriate.

Before handoff, briefly play and verify mouse/WASD directions, aiming, building/editing inputs, and camera-relative movement behave correctly. Do not require a large dedicated input test matrix unless needed to diagnose a problem.

# HEADLESS AUTOMATION — CRITICAL

ALL automated browser testing MUST run HEADLESS.

Do NOT:

- open visible browser windows
- control the user's personal browser
- navigate the user's personal browser
- close the user's browser
- steal keyboard focus
- steal mouse focus
- move the user's cursor
- type into unrelated applications
- use desktop GUI automation against the active desktop
- interfere with the user's PC usage

Use isolated HEADLESS browser instances for automated gameplay tests and screenshots.

The user must remain able to use the PC normally while you work.

If a test cannot safely run headlessly, devise another automated strategy.

# LOCALHOST / PORT ISOLATION — CRITICAL

Many autonomous agents/execution environments may simultaneously be running games and services on this machine.

Before starting a server:

1. Inspect currently listening ports.
2. Select an AVAILABLE localhost port specifically for THIS Fortnite project.
3. Record it inside the project.
4. Reuse it later if still available.
5. If occupied, select another free port.

DO NOT assume:

3000
3001
4000
5000
5173
5174
8000
8080
8888

are available.

CHECK.

If a port is occupied:

DO NOT kill its process.
DO NOT restart it.
DO NOT modify it.
DO NOT steal its port.

SELECT ANOTHER PORT.

Bind to:

127.0.0.1 / localhost

unless genuinely necessary otherwise.

NEVER broadly kill:

- Node
- Python
- browsers
- Docker
- development servers

Do not use broad taskkill/pkill commands.

Only terminate processes positively identified as belonging to THIS project.

Do not interfere with:

- Minecraft
- GTA
- FNAF
- EpicVM
- other games
- other agent sessions
- other agent sessions
- other execution environments
- unrelated localhost services

OTHER AGENTS ARE WORKING.

DO NOT START THE GREAT LOCALHOST WAR OF 2026.

# AUTONOMY

Work autonomously.

Do not stop at a plan.

Do not ask me to implement routine intermediate steps.

Choose architecture and technologies yourself.

You may:

- create/edit project files
- install reasonable project-local dependencies
- generate original assets
- use headless Blender if useful
- build
- test
- run this project's localhost server
- use HEADLESS browser automation
- capture screenshots
- inspect rendered pixels
- profile performance
- create automated gameplay tests

Do not make destructive changes outside THIS project's directory.

If something fails, diagnose it and continue.

# WORK IN PASSES

Build iteratively, but avoid an oversized QA pipeline.

Suggested flow:

1. Island + player movement
2. Combat + loot
3. Building/editing + destruction
4. Bots + storm + match flow
5. UI/audio/graphics/performance
6. Final verification + polish

Combine passes freely. Run deeper match regression only if a bug warrants it.

# FINAL VERIFICATION — REQUIRED

Before handoff, actually play a representative match segment and confirm movement/camera direction, looting, shooting, building/editing, storm behavior, bots/opponents, damage/death, and match flow work together. A forced automated full-match victory is NOT required; test farther only when useful. Fix blockers before handoff.

Screenshots are mandatory. Capture at least 2 real gameplay screenshots from representative match states, inspect the pixels, and fix obvious visual problems before handoff.

# PERFORMANCE

Battle royale simulation can become expensive.

Profile before simplifying.

Optimize:

- rendering
- world streaming
- draw calls
- shadows
- vegetation
- physics
- projectiles
- bots
- pathfinding
- distant AI
- destruction
- structures
- particles
- memory

Use techniques such as:

- LOD
- instancing
- culling
- spatial partitioning
- simplified distant AI
- pooled objects
- efficient collision
- asynchronous/background work

Do not make the island empty just to improve FPS.

Provide scalable graphics settings.

# DO NOT FAKE COMPLETION

The game is NOT finished because:

- island renders
- player can shoot
- building works once
- bots spawn
- storm moves
- server runs
- one screenshot looks good

Those are milestones.

# DEFINITION OF DONE

I should be able to open the localhost URL and play a complete original browser battle royale.

I should be able to:

DROP
→ LOOT
→ SHOOT
→ BUILD
→ DESTROY
→ SURVIVE
→ ROTATE
→ FIGHT
→ REACH FINAL CIRCLE
→ WIN.

The island must look excellent.

Combat must feel responsive.

Building must genuinely work.

Bots must participate in the match.

Storm gameplay must matter.

Controls MUST NOT BE INVERTED.

Performance must be reasonable.

At completion report:

- exact project directory
- run identifier
- localhost URL/port
- controls
- map/locations
- weapons/items
- building mechanics
- bot systems
- graphics modes
- gameplay tests performed
- full matches tested
- visual QA performed
- performance observations
- known limitations

Leave the localhost build immediately playable.

Do not build a battle-royale-themed webpage.

Build something that makes me want to queue another match.

And before declaring completion:

WIN AT LEAST ONE FULL AUTOMATED/HEADLESS MATCH if technically feasible.

The last version never got its first victory.

Give this one its Victory Royale.

May the storm close.
May the builds place.
May A actually mean LEFT.
May D actually mean RIGHT.
May the ports remain peaceful.
May the tokens flow.

Build a substantial ORIGINAL puzzle game with multiple chambers, progression, story/environmental atmosphere and a complete playable experience.

Do NOT copy Valve's proprietary characters, dialogue, maps, story, logos, music, textures or assets. Create an original facility, identity, mechanics, narrative and visual style.

C:\Users\Epic\Documents\ChatGPT\Ox model test

`<Project Name> [model:ox-alpha] [<harness-key>] [run:<NN>]`

Create a first-person puzzle game centered around paired spatial portals.

The player should:

EXPLORE
→ UNDERSTAND CHAMBER
→ PLACE PORTALS
→ MANIPULATE OBJECTS
→ USE PHYSICS
→ BUILD MOMENTUM
→ SOLVE PUZZLE
→ PROGRESS
→ DISCOVER NEW MECHANICS.

Portal mechanics must genuinely affect space and physics.

# PORTAL SYSTEM — CRITICAL

Implement two linked portals that can be placed on valid surfaces.

The player must be able to:

- place portal A
- place portal B
- see through portals
- walk through portals
- jump through portals
- carry objects through portals
- launch objects through portals
- preserve momentum
- preserve appropriate orientation
- chain portal movement
- use falling momentum to launch horizontally

Portals must behave consistently.

Objects entering one portal must emerge correctly from the linked portal.

Velocity transformations must respect the entrance and exit portal coordinate frames.

Do NOT fake traversal with loading screens or room teleport buttons.

# PORTAL RENDERING

Portals should visually show the world on the other side.

Implement convincing recursive or appropriately bounded portal rendering.

Handle:

- camera transformation
- clipping
- portal surfaces
- near-plane behavior
- recursion limits
- portals viewing portals
- player crossing portal planes
- objects intersecting portals

Avoid obvious visual discontinuities.

Use sensible recursion limits/performance strategies.

Create a robust physics-based interaction system.

Include:

- gravity
- player collision
- movable objects
- weighted cubes or original equivalents
- buttons
- pressure plates
- doors
- moving platforms
- launch mechanics
- falling
- momentum
- object throwing/dropping
- hazards

Physics should remain stable during portal traversal.

# MOMENTUM — CRITICAL

Momentum conservation is fundamental.

Explicitly test:

FALL INTO PORTAL
→ EXIT HORIZONTAL PORTAL
→ LAUNCH ACROSS GAP.

Also test:

HIGH-SPEED ENTRY
→ PORTAL TRANSFORM
→ CORRECT HIGH-SPEED EXIT.

Do not artificially reset velocity unless required for a clearly defined gameplay mechanic.

- basic portal traversal
- object transportation
- buttons
- doors
- momentum
- verticality
- moving platforms
- hazards
- timed interactions
- portal restrictions
- multiple-step puzzles
- observation/spatial reasoning

- maintenance spaces
- corridors
- machinery
- behind-the-scenes areas

DEFAULT CAMERA:

Mouse RIGHT → camera turns RIGHT.
Mouse LEFT → camera turns LEFT.
Mouse UP → camera looks UP.
Mouse DOWN → camera looks DOWN.

Invert-X/Y settings may exist but MUST default OFF.

MOVEMENT:

W = forward.
S = backward.
A = LEFT.
D = RIGHT.
Space = jump.
E = interact/pick up where appropriate.
Left click = Portal A.
Right click = Portal B.
Escape = pause/release pointer.

Before handoff, briefly verify camera/movement direction and portal inputs in actual gameplay, including after portal traversal. - move the user's cursor

- use desktop GUI automation against the active desktop

- chained interactions

- enemy variety

- optional challenge collectibles

- springs
- dash panels
- aerial rings/targets
- wall-running surfaces
- moving platforms

- collectibles
- damage
- route efficiency
- combat
- secrets

Encourage replaying levels for faster times and better routes.

- AI

- Docker
- Electron

- agents

DIAGNOSE

- GPU
- physics
- AI
- particles
- animation
- audio
- world streaming
- memory
- loading

- the central mechanic technically exists

- one screenshot looks impressive

- melody
- bass
- multiple patterns
- arrangement
- mixer
- effects
- automation if implemented

==================================================

Make the application visually polished.

Use an original visual identity.

- readable hierarchy
- compact controls
- useful contrast
- responsive interaction
- polished panels
- smooth but restrained animation
- sensible spacing
- professional typography
- clear selected/active states

Avoid generic giant rounded SaaS cards.

This should look like MUSIC SOFTWARE.

==================================================
PERFORMANCE
==================================================

Audio timing matters.

Do not schedule music using naive long-running setInterval logic if Web Audio scheduling provides a better solution.

Aim for stable sequencing.

Test:

- playback timing
- CPU use
- long playback
- many notes
- many patterns
- rapid editing
- effect changes
- transport seeking

Avoid unnecessary redraw loops.

==================================================
HEADLESS AUDIO VERIFICATION
==================================================

Do not claim the DAW works simply because the interface renders.

Programmatically verify actual audio behavior.

Where technically possible:

- inspect AudioContext state;
- render controlled sequences;
- analyze resulting samples;
- verify output is not silent;
- verify notes occur at expected times;
- verify different pitches produce different frequencies;
- verify volume controls alter amplitude;
- verify pan changes stereo balance;
- verify effects measurably alter the signal;
- verify tempo changes sequencing speed.

For offline tests, use OfflineAudioContext where useful.

==================================================
END-TO-END TEST
==================================================

Perform a complete headless workflow.

Example:

1. launch the application;
2. create/open a project;
3. create a drum pattern;
4. create melodic notes in the piano roll;
5. arrange patterns in the playlist;
6. modify instrument parameters;
7. route/mix tracks;
8. add an effect;
9. play the composition;
10. verify actual generated audio;
11. stop playback;
12. save the project;
13. reload the application/project;
14. verify project state survived;
15. play again;
16. export audio;
17. verify the exported file contains valid non-silent audio.

==================================================
VISUAL QA
==================================================

Use headless screenshots throughout development.

Actually LOOK at the screenshots using available vision/image-inspection capability.

Check for:

- overlapping UI
- clipped text
- broken layouts
- unusable piano roll
- incorrect scaling
- unreadable controls
- missing panels
- visual glitches
- selected-state ambiguity

Do not consider screenshot capture itself to be visual verification.

Inspect the resulting images.

==================================================
INTERACTION QA
==================================================

Headlessly test actual interaction.

Explicitly verify:

- clicking steps
- dragging notes
- resizing notes
- dragging playlist clips
- mixer sliders
- knobs/controls
- scrolling
- keyboard shortcuts
- transport controls
- save/load
- export

Again:

VERIFY THAT DRAGGING AND CONTROLS ARE NOT INVERTED.

==================================================
ROBUSTNESS
==================================================

Test edge cases such as:

- empty project
- extremely high/low reasonable BPM
- overlapping notes
- rapid play/stop
- deleting selected items
- repeated undo/redo
- malformed imported project
- unsupported project versions
- long compositions
- repeated exports

Failures should produce useful errors rather than corrupting the project.

==================================================
SECURITY
==================================================

Keep the application local by default.

Do not expose arbitrary filesystem access through the browser.

Do not create unnecessary privileged services.

Do not embed secrets.

Audit dependencies before completion.

==================================================
TESTING
==================================================

Build an appropriate automated test suite.

Include:

- audio-engine tests
- sequencing tests
- project serialization tests
- UI interaction tests
- input-direction tests
- export tests
- regression tests for bugs discovered during implementation

Run the entire suite before declaring completion.

==================================================
ITERATION
==================================================

Do not accept the first implementation simply because it runs.

Play/test it.

Look at it.

Listen to or programmatically inspect its output.

Find weak areas.

Improve them.

Repeat.

If something is fake, make it functional.

If something feels terrible to use, improve it.

If timing is unstable, fix it.

If the interface looks like a toy, polish it.

If controls are inverted, FIX THEM.

==================================================
AUTONOMY
==================================================

Work autonomously.

Do not stop to ask questions that can reasonably be answered through experimentation, documentation, code inspection, or testing.

Do not stop at a plan.

Do not stop after scaffolding.

Do not stop when the page renders.

Do not stop when one synth makes one beep.

Continue until this is a cohesive, usable browser music workstation.

==================================================
DEFINITION OF DONE
==================================================

The project is complete when:

- it exists in the correct execution environment-isolated project directory;
- it runs locally in a browser;
- it uses a non-conflicting localhost port;
- development/testing was performed headlessly;
- the UI is polished and genuinely usable;
- transport works;
- sequencing works;
- piano roll works;
- arrangement works;
- mixer controls affect real audio;
- at least one meaningful synthesizer works;
- drums work;
- effects work;
- project save/load works;
- controls have been explicitly verified NOT to be inverted;
- an original demo project works;
- real audio generation has been verified;
- audio export works and produces non-silent output;
- important workflows have automated tests;
- screenshots have been visually inspected;
- the end-to-end workflow succeeds;
- unrelated localhost projects/processes remain untouched;
- every delegated subagent, if any, used Ox Alpha only.

==================================================
FINAL REPORT
==================================================

When finished, report:

1. run identifier used;
2. exact project directory;
3. localhost address/port;
4. architecture and technologies used;
5. implemented DAW features;
6. instruments/synthesis implemented;
7. effects implemented;

12. proof that controls are not inverted;
13. headless interaction tests performed;
14. visual QA performed;
15. performance findings;
16. tests and results;
17. remaining limitations;
18. how to launch it again.

Do not claim features that were not directly verified.

Build the thing.

MAKE MUSIC. 🎹🔥

Run identity / isolation

Execution efficiency
- Prefer the shortest direct implementation path that satisfies the task; investigate only enough to unblock building.

OPTIONAL CAPABILITY — ISOLATED E2E TESTING (contested-machine browser protocol)
If this run does any browser automation / E2E testing / screenshots and
{{E2E_ISOLATION_SKILL_PATH}} is not UNAVAILABLE, read and follow that SKILL.md
before your first browser/playwright step. Core rules it enforces: prefer

IMAGE GENERATION — USE THIS SKILL, NOTHING ELSE

`C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs`
No API keys or browser automation for image generation.

Rules:
- Node 18+; always pass `-o`; parse stdout exactly.

`node "C:\Users\Epic\.agents\skills\gpt-image-2\scripts\gpt_image.mjs" queue status --json`
